Financial Statement Analysis (FSA)

The definitive, curriculum-complete master study guide synthesized for CFA® Level 1 and Level 2 candidates. Covering all foundational accounting mechanics, advanced corporate consolidations, multinational currency translations, pensions, financial institution models, forensic quality frameworks, and interactive visual charts.

CFA Exam Syllabus (L1 & L2) 30-40 Page Comprehensive Scope Interactive Visual Charts IFRS vs US GAAP Master Matrix

01. Introduction to FSA & Mechanics

Financial Statement Analysis provides analysts with the quantitative foundation to assess a company's past performance, current financial position, risk profile, and future cash flow generating capabilities.

The Accounting Equation & Double-Entry Accounting

Core Accounting Identity
$$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Contributed Capital} + \text{Ending Retained Earnings}$$ $$\text{Ending Retained Earnings} = \text{Beginning Retained Earnings} + \text{Net Income} - \text{Dividends Declared}$$

Every transaction affects at least two accounts (debits must equal credits). Under accrual accounting, revenues are recognized when earned and expenses when incurred, decoupling accounting profit from immediate cash inflows and outflows.

The Financial Statement Framework (Core 4 Statements)

  1. Balance Sheet (Statement of Financial Position): Snapshot of what a company owns (assets) and owes (liabilities and equity) at a specific point in time.
  2. Income Statement (Statement of Comprehensive Income): Measures financial performance over a specified duration (revenues minus expenses).
  3. Statement of Cash Flows: Reconciles beginning and ending cash balances across Operating, Investing, and Financing activities over a period.
  4. Statement of Changes in Equity: Details movements in contributed capital, retained earnings, and accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI).

Auditor Opinions Spectrum

Audit Opinion Meaning / Circumstances Analyst Implication
Unqualified (Clean) Financial statements are presented fairly in all material respects conforming with GAAP/IFRS. High reliability of baseline reporting. Standard baseline for analysis.
Qualified Statements are fairly presented except for a specific, isolated departure or scope limitation. Carefully inspect footnote explanations regarding the exception. Adjust models.
Adverse Financial statements as a whole are materially misstated or non-compliant. Severe Red Flag. Financial data cannot be relied upon for valuation.
Disclaimer of Opinion Auditor is unable to form an opinion due to severe scope limitation or lack of independence. Extreme risk. Company management may be withholding critical solvency data.

02. Financial Reporting Standards & Framework

Financial reporting standards provide consistency, comparability, and transparency across global capital markets. The two dominant global standard setters are the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) and the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB).

The IASB Conceptual Framework (Qualitative Characteristics)

Category Characteristic Core Definition & Application
Fundamental Characteristics
(Must be present for information to be useful)		 Relevance Information has predictive value, confirmatory value, or both. Must be material (omission alters user decision).
Faithful Representation Information is complete, neutral (free from bias), and free from material error.
Enhancing Characteristics
(Increases utility of relevant & faithful data)		 Comparability Allows users to identify real similarities and differences across companies and across time.
Verifiability Different knowledgeable and independent observers can reach a consensus that a representation is faithful.
Timeliness Information is available to decision-makers in time to influence their economic evaluations.
Understandability Information is classified, characterized, and presented clearly and concisely for diligent users.
⚠️ The Pervasive Cost Constraint

The benefits of financial reporting information must always exceed the costs of providing and using that information. Standard setters do not mandate disclosure if compliance costs outweigh decision-making utility.

03. Understanding Income Statements

The Income Statement reports the financial performance of an entity over a period, reflecting operational revenues, expenses, financing costs, and taxes.

Revenue Recognition: The 5-Step Model (IFRS 15 & ASC 606)

  1. Identify the contract(s) with a customer (commercial substance, rights, and collectability).
  2. Identify the distinct performance obligations in the contract.
  3. Determine the transaction price (considering variable consideration, discounts, and financing terms).
  4. Allocate the transaction price to performance obligations based on relative standalone selling prices.
  5. Recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies a performance obligation (point in time vs. over time).

Earnings Per Share (EPS): Basic and Diluted

Basic EPS
$$\text{Basic EPS} = \frac{\text{Net Income} - \text{Preferred Dividends}}{\text{Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares (WACS)}}$$

When potentially dilutive securities (convertible bonds, convertible preferred stock, stock options, warrants) exist, Diluted EPS must be calculated:

Diluted EPS Formula
$$\text{Diluted EPS} = \frac{\text{Net Income} - \text{Pref Div} + \text{Pref Div on Conv Pref} + \text{Conv Debt Interest}(1 - t)}{\text{WACS} + \text{Shares from Conv Pref} + \text{Shares from Conv Debt} + \text{Net Shares from Options (Treasury Stock Method)}}$$
💡 The Treasury Stock Method for Options & Warrants

Assumes proceeds from exercising in-the-money options are used to repurchase shares at the average market price over the period:

$$\Delta \text{Shares} = \text{Options} \times \left(1 - \frac{\text{Exercise Price}}{\text{Average Market Price}}\right)$$

If the calculated Diluted EPS is greater than Basic EPS, the security is anti-dilutive and must be excluded from Diluted EPS reporting.

Comprehensive Income & Other Comprehensive Income (OCI)

Comprehensive Income includes Net Income plus Other Comprehensive Income (OCI). Key items bypassing the Income Statement and entering OCI directly under the PUFE acronym:

  • P: Pension adjustments (actuarial gains/losses and prior service costs under US GAAP; re-measurements under IFRS).
  • U: Unrealized holding gains/losses on available-for-sale (FVOCI) debt securities.
  • F: Foreign currency translation adjustments (Cumulative Translation Adjustment - CTA under Current Rate method).
  • E: Effective portion of cash flow hedge gains/losses.

04. Understanding Balance Sheets

The Balance Sheet displays the financial structure of the firm, revealing liquidity, capital resources, and asset composition.

Measurement Bases of Assets & Liabilities

  • Historical Cost: Initial acquisition consideration plus costs to prepare asset for use (objective, verifiable, but lacks market relevance over time).
  • Amortized Cost: Historical cost adjusted for cumulative depreciation, amortization, depletion, and impairment.
  • Fair Value: Exit price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants.
  • Net Realizable Value (NRV): Estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business less estimated completion and selling costs.

Tangible vs. Intangible Assets & Goodwill

Internally generated intangible assets (e.g., brand value, patents developed in-house):

  • US GAAP: All Research and Development (R&D) costs must be expensed as incurred (with narrow exceptions for software development after technological feasibility).
  • IFRS: Research phase costs are expensed; Development phase costs are capitalized once commercial feasibility, technical viability, and economic benefit are demonstrated.

Goodwill arises only in business combinations when purchase consideration exceeds the fair value of net identifiable assets acquired. Goodwill is never amortized under IFRS or US GAAP; it is tested annually for impairment.

05. Understanding Cash Flow Statements

The Cash Flow Statement eliminates accrual adjustments to show literal cash generated and used across three primary categories: Operating (CFO), Investing (CFI), and Financing (CFF).

Direct vs. Indirect Method for Cash Flow from Operations (CFO)

Method Mechanism Conversion Adjustments
Direct Method Lists gross cash receipts (cash collected from customers) and gross cash disbursements (cash paid to suppliers, employees, interest, taxes). $$\text{Cash Collected} = \text{Sales} - \Delta \text{AR} + \Delta \text{Unearned Rev}$$ $$\text{Cash Paid to Suppliers} = \text{COGS} + \Delta \text{Inv} - \Delta \text{AP}$$
Indirect Method Starts with Net Income, adds back non-cash expenses (depreciation, amortization), adjusts for non-operating items (gains/losses on sale), and adds/subtracts changes in working capital accounts. $$\text{CFO} = \text{Net Income} + \text{Depr/Amort} - \text{Gain on Sale} + \text{Loss on Sale} - \Delta \text{Current Assets} + \Delta \text{Current Liabilities}$$

Classification Differences: IFRS vs. US GAAP

Cash Flow Item US GAAP Classification IFRS Allowed Classifications
Interest Paid Operating (CFO) Operating (CFO) or Financing (CFF)
Interest Received Operating (CFO) Operating (CFO) or Investing (CFI)
Dividends Paid Financing (CFF) Financing (CFF) or Operating (CFO)
Dividends Received Operating (CFO) Operating (CFO) or Investing (CFI)
Taxes Paid Operating (CFO) Operating (unless specific to CFI or CFF)

Free Cash Flow: FCFF and FCFE

Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF)
$$\text{FCFF} = \text{CFO} + \text{Interest Expense} \times (1 - \text{Tax Rate}) - \text{FCInv}$$ $$\text{FCFF} = \text{NI} + \text{NCC} + \text{Int} \times (1 - t) - \text{FCInv} - \text{WCInv}$$
Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE)
$$\text{FCFE} = \text{CFO} - \text{FCInv} + \text{Net Borrowing}$$

06. Financial Analysis Techniques & DuPont

Financial ratios standardize financial statement data to assess liquidity, activity, solvency, profitability, and return metrics across entities regardless of absolute size.

DuPont Return on Equity (ROE) Decomposition

3-Step DuPont Analysis
$$\text{ROE} = \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Net Income}}{\text{Revenue}}\right)}_{\text{Net Profit Margin}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Revenue}}{\text{Total Assets}}\right)}_{\text{Asset Turnover}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Total Assets}}{\text{Equity}}\right)}_{\text{Financial Leverage Ratio}}$$
5-Step Extended DuPont Analysis
$$\text{ROE} = \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Net Income}}{\text{EBT}}\right)}_{\text{Tax Burden}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{EBT}}{\text{EBIT}}\right)}_{\text{Interest Burden}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{EBIT}}{\text{Revenue}}\right)}_{\text{Operating Margin}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Revenue}}{\text{Total Assets}}\right)}_{\text{Asset Turnover}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Total Assets}}{\text{Equity}}\right)}_{\text{Financial Leverage}}$$
Visual 1: DuPont 5-Step Return Drivers Comparison
Relative component contributions between an operational leader vs. a debt-leveraged firm.

Key Ratio Reference Handbook

Classification Ratio Name Formula Analytical Interpretation
Liquidity Current Ratio $\frac{\text{Current Assets}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}$ Short-term debt-paying capability. Normal range: 1.2x – 2.0x.
Quick (Acid-Test) Ratio $\frac{\text{Cash} + \text{Marketable Securities} + \text{Receivables}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}$ Excludes illiquid inventory and prepaid expenses.
Cash Ratio $\frac{\text{Cash} + \text{Marketable Securities}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}$ Most conservative measure of ultra-liquid cash reserves.
Activity / Efficiency Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) $\frac{365}{\text{Receivables Turnover}} = \frac{\text{AR} \times 365}{\text{Revenue}}$ Average collection time in days. Rising DSO signals collection issues.
Days of Inventory on Hand (DOH) $\frac{365}{\text{Inventory Turnover}} = \frac{\text{Inventory} \times 365}{\text{COGS}}$ Average shelf duration. Rising DOH implies obsolete stock or slowdown.
Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) $\text{DOH} + \text{DSO} - \text{Days of Payables Outstanding (DPO)}$ Net timeframe from cash investment in inventory to collection of cash.
Solvency Debt-to-Equity $\frac{\text{Total Debt}}{\text{Total Shareholders' Equity}}$ Long-term capital structure reliance on creditors vs owners.
Interest Coverage (Times Interest Earned) $\frac{\text{EBIT}}{\text{Interest Payments}}$ Ability to service periodic debt interest obligations out of earnings.

07. Inventories (FIFO, LIFO & Valuation)

Inventory valuation significantly influences Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), gross margins, taxable income, and balance sheet working capital.

Cost Flow Methods Under Inflationary Conditions

  • FIFO (First-In, First-Out): Assigns earliest costs to COGS; ending inventory reflects recent market prices. Under inflation: lower COGS $\rightarrow$ higher Net Income $\rightarrow$ higher income taxes $\rightarrow$ lower operating cash flow.
  • LIFO (Last-In, First-Out): Assigns latest costs to COGS; ending inventory reflects older historic prices. Permitted only under US GAAP (strictly prohibited under IFRS). Under inflation: higher COGS $\rightarrow$ lower Net Income $\rightarrow$ lower taxes $\rightarrow$ higher operating cash flow (tax savings).
  • Weighted Average Cost: Assigns average unit cost across all inventory available for sale. Results fall strictly between FIFO and LIFO.
Visual 2: Financial Statement Impact under Inflation (Rising Prices)
Comparison of financial outcomes across FIFO, Weighted Average, and LIFO cost methods.

LIFO Reserve and LIFO Liquidation Formulas

To compare a LIFO-reporting firm with a FIFO competitor, analysts must adjust using the LIFO Reserve disclosed in footnotes:

LIFO to FIFO Conversions
$$\text{Inventory}_{\text{FIFO}} = \text{Inventory}_{\text{LIFO}} + \text{LIFO Reserve}$$ $$\text{COGS}_{\text{FIFO}} = \text{COGS}_{\text{LIFO}} - \Delta \text{LIFO Reserve}$$ $$\text{Retained Earnings}_{\text{FIFO}} = \text{Retained Earnings}_{\text{LIFO}} + \text{LIFO Reserve} \times (1 - \text{Tax Rate})$$
🚨 LIFO Liquidation Risk

Occurs when inventory unit sales exceed unit purchases, forcing older, lower-cost inventory layers into COGS. This artificially compresses COGS, generates an unsustainable spike in gross profit and net income, and creates a substantial income tax liability.

Lower of Cost and Net Realizable Value / Market

Standard Measurement Floor / Ceiling Impairment Reversal Allowed?
IFRS Lower of Cost or Net Realizable Value (NRV = Estimated Sales Price - Completion/Selling Costs). Yes (Permitted up to the original cost amount).
US GAAP (FIFO / Weighted Avg) Lower of Cost or Net Realizable Value (NRV). No (Strictly prohibited).
US GAAP (LIFO / Retail) Lower of Cost or Market (Market = Replacement cost bounded by Ceiling [NRV] and Floor [NRV - Normal Profit Margin]). No (Strictly prohibited).

08. Long-Lived Assets & Depreciation

Accounting for property, plant, and equipment (PPE) and intangible assets impacts asset base size, operating margins, and cash flow classifications.

Capitalizing vs. Expensing Costs

Financial Metric Capitalizing Expenditure Expensing Immediately
Initial Net Income Higher (cost deferred via balance sheet) Lower (entire cost hits P&L immediately)
Subsequent Net Income Lower (due to ongoing depreciation/amortization) Higher (no future depreciation burden)
Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) Higher (cash outflow classified as CFI) Lower (cash outflow classified as CFO)
Total Assets & Equity Higher in initial years Lower in initial years

Depreciation Mechanics

Straight-Line Depreciation
$$\text{Annual Expense} = \frac{\text{Historical Cost} - \text{Residual Value}}{\text{Useful Life}}$$
Double-Declining Balance (DDB) Depreciation
$$\text{Expense}_t = \text{Carrying Value at Start of Year } t \times \left(\frac{2}{\text{Useful Life}}\right)$$ (Note: Salvage value is not deducted when computing annual expense, but asset is never depreciated below salvage value).
Visual 3: Carrying Value Trajectories by Depreciation Method
Asset carrying amount over 5-year useful life (Cost: 100,000 USD; Salvage: 10,000 USD).

IFRS Revaluation Model vs. US GAAP Cost Model

Under IFRS, companies may choose the Revaluation Model for entire asset classes:

  • If revaluation increases carrying value: Initial gain bypasses P&L and goes directly to Revaluation Surplus in OCI (unless reversing a prior loss recognized in P&L).
  • If revaluation decreases carrying value: Loss is recognized in P&L to the extent it exceeds previous revaluation surplus in OCI.
  • US GAAP strictly mandates the Cost Model; revaluation upward to fair value is prohibited.

Impairment of Long-Lived Assets

  • IFRS: Impairment occurs when Carrying Value exceeds Recoverable Amount (Higher of: Fair Value less costs to sell, and Value in Use [PV of future cash flows]). Impairment write-downs can be reversed up to historical cost.
  • US GAAP: 2-step test. Step 1 (Recoverability test): If undiscounted future cash flows $<$ Carrying Value, asset is impaired. Step 2 (Loss measurement): Impairment Loss = Carrying Value $-$ Fair Value. Impairment write-downs for assets held for use cannot be reversed.

09. Income Taxes (DTAs, DTLs & Tax Rates)

Differences between accounting rules (IFRS/US GAAP) and tax legislation generate disparities between Accounting Profit and Taxable Income.

Core Tax Terminology

  • Income Tax Expense: P&L tax expense = Current Tax Payable $+$ $\Delta$DTL $-$ $\Delta$DTA.
  • Current Tax Payable: Actual cash liability owed to tax authorities based on Taxable Income.
  • Deferred Tax Asset (DTA): Future tax savings created when Taxable Income $>$ Accounting Profit (e.g., tax paid early, warranty accruals, loss carryforwards).
  • Deferred Tax Liability (DTL): Future tax payable created when Accounting Profit $>$ Taxable Income (e.g., accelerated tax depreciation vs straight-line book depreciation).
Balance Sheet Approach to Deferred Taxes
$$\text{Temporary Difference} = \text{Carrying Value (Book)} - \text{Tax Base}$$ $$\text{If Book Asset} > \text{Tax Base Asset} \implies \mathbf{DTL}$$ $$\text{If Book Asset} < \text{Tax Base Asset} \implies \mathbf{DTA}$$ $$\text{If Book Liability} > \text{Tax Base Liability} \implies \mathbf{DTA}$$ $$\text{If Book Liability} < \text{Tax Base Liability} \implies \mathbf{DTL}$$

Valuation Allowances & Tax Rate Revisions

Under US GAAP, a Valuation Allowance contra-account reduces DTA if it is "more likely than not" ($>50\%$ probability) that some or all of the DTA will not be realized through future taxable profits. (IFRS reduces DTA carrying value directly).

⚠️ Effect of Tax Rate Changes on Existing DTA/DTL

When the enacted statutory tax rate decreases:

  • Existing DTL balances decrease $\rightarrow$ Increases Net Income in P&L.
  • Existing DTA balances decrease $\rightarrow$ Decreases Net Income in P&L.

10. Non-Current Liabilities & Bonds

Corporate debt financing through bonds payable involves tracking coupon payments, interest expense, and liability amortization.

Bond Issuance Pricing Dynamics

  • Par Bond: Coupon Rate $=$ Market Yield at Issuance (YTM). Book Value remains at Face Value.
  • Discount Bond: Coupon Rate $<$ Market Yield. Issued below par; Carrying value increases over life toward par. Interest Expense $>$ Coupon Paid.
  • Premium Bond: Coupon Rate $>$ Market Yield. Issued above par; Carrying value decreases over life toward par. Interest Expense $<$ Coupon Paid.
Effective Interest Rate Method
$$\text{Periodic Interest Expense} = \text{Carrying Value at Start of Period} \times \text{Market Yield at Issuance}$$ $$\text{Coupon Paid} = \text{Face (Par) Value} \times \text{Stated Coupon Rate}$$ $$\Delta \text{Carrying Value} = \text{Interest Expense} - \text{Coupon Paid}$$
Visual 4: Bond Carrying Value Convergence to Par
Evolution of Carrying Amount over 5 years for Discount (8% coupon, 10% yield) vs Premium (12% coupon, 10% yield) bonds.

Debt Derecognition (Extinguishment)

When debt is retired early before maturity:

$$\text{Gain or Loss on Extinguishment} = \text{Carrying Value of Debt} - \text{Reacquisition Price Paid}$$

Recognized as an ordinary gain or loss in the Income Statement.

11. Leases (IFRS 16 vs. ASC 842)

Under modern lease accounting standards, almost all leases are brought onto the balance sheet for lessees, ending historic off-balance sheet operating lease structures.

Lessee Accounting Comparison

Feature IFRS 16 (Single Model) US GAAP ASC 842 (Dual Model)
Balance Sheet Recognizes Right-of-Use (ROU) Asset and Lease Liability for all leases (except short-term $<12$ mos or low-value assets). Recognizes ROU Asset and Lease Liability for both Operating and Finance leases.
Income Statement Front-loaded expense: Depreciation of ROU asset (operating expense) $+$ Interest expense on lease liability (financing expense). Finance Lease: Same as IFRS (front-loaded Depreciation + Interest).
Operating Lease: Single straight-line lease expense recognized entirely in operating expenses.
Cash Flow Statement Principal portion of lease payment $\rightarrow$ CFF.
Interest portion $\rightarrow$ CFO (or CFF). 		Finance Lease: Principal in CFF; Interest in CFO.
Operating Lease: Entire lease payment in CFO.
EBITDA Impact Higher EBITDA (rent expense converted to Depreciation & Interest). Higher EBITDA for Finance leases; Unchanged for Operating leases.

12. Financial Reporting Quality Spectrum (L1)

Financial reporting quality spans a wide spectrum, ranging from pristine economic truth to outright fraudulent fabrication.

Quality Tier Characteristics
Tier 1: High Quality / High Earnings Quality GAAP/IFRS compliant, transparent, decision-useful, faithful representation, sustainable economic earnings.
Tier 2: High Quality / Low Earnings Quality GAAP/IFRS compliant and transparent, but earnings have low sustainability (high cyclicality, volatile margins, non-recurring items).
Tier 3: Biased Accounting Choices Within GAAP/IFRS rules, but aggressive (early revenue recognition, delayed expenses) or conservative (cookie-jar reserves) choices obscure performance.
Tier 4: Earnings Management Deliberate timing of real transactions or aggressive accounting discretion to manipulate reported metrics.
Tier 5: Non-Compliant / Fraudulent Departures from GAAP/IFRS, fabricated fictitious revenues, hidden liabilities, and intentional fraud.

13. Intercorporate Investments (CFA L2)

At Level 2, intercorporate investments are evaluated based on the degree of influence or control the investor company exercises over the investee.

Investment Classification Matrix

Ownership Level Typical Influence Accounting Standard / Method
$< 20\%$ Passive (No Significant Influence) IFRS 9 / ASC 321: Amortized Cost, FVOCI, or FVPL
20% – 50% Significant Influence Equity Method (One-line consolidation)
$> 50\%$ Control Acquisition Method (Full 100% consolidation)
Variable Interest Primary Beneficiary VIE / SPE Consolidation (regardless of voting rights)

The Equity Method Mechanics (20% – 50%)

Reported on the balance sheet as a single non-current asset line:

$$\text{Ending Investment Value} = \text{Initial Cost} + (\% \times \text{Investee NI}) - (\% \times \text{Investee Dividends}) - \text{Amortization of Excess Purchase Price}$$

Note: Dividends received under the equity method do not impact the investor's Net Income; they are treated as a return of capital, reducing the carrying value of the investment and appearing as CFO cash inflow.

Business Combinations: Acquisition Method ($>50\%$)

All assets and liabilities of the subsidiary are consolidated at 100% Fair Value on acquisition date. If less than 100% is purchased, Non-Controlling Interest (NCI) is established.

Goodwill Approach IFRS vs US GAAP Goodwill Calculation Formula NCI Measurement Base
Full Goodwill Permitted under IFRS; Mandatory under US GAAP $$\text{Fair Value of Subsidiary as Whole} - \text{FV of Identifiable Net Assets}$$ NCI measured at Fair Value of minority shares
Partial Goodwill Permitted under IFRS; Prohibited under US GAAP $$\text{Purchase Price Paid} - (\% \times \text{FV of Identifiable Net Assets})$$ NCI measured at minority % share of FV of net identifiable assets

14. Employee Compensation & Pensions (CFA L2)

Post-employment benefits are dominated by Defined Benefit (DB) pension plans, which require extensive actuarial valuation and complex funded status tracking.

Balance Sheet Funded Status

Net Pension Asset / Liability (Funded Status)
$$\text{Funded Status} = \text{Fair Value of Plan Assets (FVPA)} - \text{Present Value of Defined Benefit Obligation (PVDBO / PBO)}$$ $$\text{If } \text{FVPA} > \text{PBO} \implies \text{Net Pension Asset (Overfunded)}$$ $$\text{If } \text{FVPA} < \text{PBO} \implies \text{Net Pension Liability (Underfunded)}$$
Visual 5: DB Pension Plan Balance Sheet Reconciliation Flow
Evolution of PBO vs Plan Assets reflecting Service, Interest, Returns, and Benefit Outflows.

Periodic Pension Cost: IFRS (IAS 19) vs. US GAAP (ASC 715)

Pension Cost Component IFRS (IAS 19) Location US GAAP (ASC 715) Location
Current Service Cost P&L (Operating) P&L (Operating)
Past Service Cost P&L immediately in full OCI initially; amortized to P&L over employee service life
Interest / Financing Cost $$\text{Net Interest} = \text{Discount Rate} \times \text{Beginning Net Funded Status} \rightarrow \mathbf{P\&L}$$ $$\text{Interest on PBO} = \text{Discount Rate} \times \text{PBO} \rightarrow \mathbf{P\&L}$$
Expected Return on Assets Subsumed in Net Interest calculation above $$\text{Expected Return} = \text{Expected Rate} \times \text{Plan Assets} \rightarrow \mathbf{P\&L} \text{ (offset)}$$
Actuarial Gains & Losses OCI (Remeasurements); never recycled to P&L OCI initially; amortized to P&L via the 10% Corridor Method
💡 Total Periodic Pension Cost (Economic Pension Cost)

The total true economic cost to the company is identical under both standards:

$$\text{Economic Pension Cost} = \text{Ending Funded Status} - \text{Beginning Funded Status} - \text{Employer Contributions}$$

15. Multinational Operations & Currency Translation (CFA L2)

Analyzing global corporations requires translating foreign subsidiary accounts denominated in local currency into the parent firm's reporting presentation currency.

Three Functional Currency Designations

  • Local Currency: The currency of the foreign country where the subsidiary is located.
  • Functional Currency: The currency of the primary economic environment in which the subsidiary operates and generates cash.
  • Presentation (Reporting) Currency: The currency in which the parent entity prepares its consolidated financial statements.

Current Rate Method vs. Temporal Method Decision Matrix

Condition Applicable Translation Method Location of Translation Gain/Loss
Functional Currency $\neq$ Presentation Currency
(Usually: Functional = Local)		 Current Rate Method Balance Sheet OCI
(Cumulative Translation Adjustment - CTA)

(Subsidiary is well-integrated with parent)		 Temporal Method (Remeasurement) Income Statement (Net Income)
Hyperinflationary Economy
(Cumulative inflation $\ge 100\%$ over 3 yrs)		 IFRS: Restate for inflation (IAS 29), then translate at Current Rate.

Balance Sheet & Income Statement Translation Rules

Account Category Current Rate Method Temporal Method
Monetary Assets & Liabilities (Cash, AR, AP, Debt) Current Rate Current Rate
Non-Monetary Assets (Inventory, PPE, Intangibles) Current Rate Historical Rate (Rate at purchase date)
Common Stock & Equity Historical Rate Historical Rate

Visual 6: FX Translation Method Exposure & Margin Volatility
Financial Statement impact when foreign currency appreciates against the presentation currency.

16. Analysis of Financial Institutions (CFA L2)

Financial institutions (banks, insurance companies) hold highly leveraged balance sheets comprised mostly of financial contracts, requiring specialized analytic frameworks.

The CAMELS Bank Evaluation Framework

  • C - Capital Adequacy: Risk-weighted capital adequacy ratios (Basel III standards).
  • A - Asset Quality: Credit risk, Non-Performing Loans (NPLs), allowance for loan losses.
  • M - Management Capabilities: Risk governance, internal controls, regulatory compliance track record.
  • E - Earnings Quality: High Net Interest Margin (NIM), sustainable fee-based income, low reliance on non-recurring trading gains.
  • L - Liquidity Position: Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR).
  • S - Sensitivity to Market Risk: Asset-liability duration matching and Value-at-Risk (VaR) exposures.

Basel III Regulatory Capital Structure

Basel III Minimum Capital Ratios (relative to Risk-Weighted Assets - RWA)
$$\text{Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1)} \ge 4.5\%$$ $$\text{Total Tier 1 Capital (CET1 + Additional Tier 1)} \ge 6.0\%$$ $$\text{Total Capital (Tier 1 + Tier 2 Capital)} \ge 8.0\%$$

Insurance Company Key Performance Indicators

Property & Casualty (P&C) Underwriting Ratios
$$\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Claims Paid} + \Delta \text{Loss Reserves}}{\text{Net Premiums Earned}}$$ $$\text{Expense Ratio} = \frac{\text{Underwriting \& Acquisition Expenses}}{\text{Net Premiums Written}}$$ $$\mathbf{\text{Combined Ratio}} = \text{Loss Ratio} + \text{Expense Ratio}$$

A Combined Ratio $< 100\%$ indicates underwriting profitability before taking into account investment returns on float.

17. Evaluating Quality of Financial Reports & Beneish M-Score

Forensic financial analysis evaluates whether reported numbers reflect genuine underlying economics or manager distortion.

The Beneish M-Score Model for Earnings Manipulation

A probit model that evaluates 8 quantitative metrics to estimate the probability that a company has manipulated its earnings. An M-Score greater than $-1.78$ (e.g., $-1.20$) indicates a high probability of manipulation.

Variable Name & Calculation Manipulation Red Flag Condition
DSRI Days Sales in Receivables Index: $\frac{\text{DSO}_t}{\text{DSO}_{t-1}}$ $>1.0$: Receivables growing faster than sales (channel stuffing, unearned revenue booking).
GMI Gross Margin Index: $\frac{\text{Gross Margin}_{t-1}}{\text{Gross Margin}_t}$ $>1.0$: Deteriorating margins create pressure to engage in earnings manipulation.
AQI Asset Quality Index: $\frac{[1 - (\text{Current Assets}_t + \text{PPE}_t + \text{Securities}_t) / \text{Total Assets}_t]}{[1 - (\text{Current Assets}_{t-1} + \text{PPE}_{t-1} + \text{Securities}_{t-1}) / \text{Total Assets}_{t-1}]}$ $>1.0$: Increasing proportion of non-current intangible/deferred costs capitalized on balance sheet.
SGI Sales Growth Index: $\frac{\text{Sales}_t}{\text{Sales}_{t-1}}$ $>1.0$: High growth companies face enormous market pressure when growth slows.
DEPI Depreciation Index: $\frac{\text{Depreciation Rate}_{t-1}}{\text{Depreciation Rate}_t}$ $>1.0$: Slowdown in depreciation rate indicates extension of asset lives to boost earnings.
SGAI SG&A Expense Index: $\frac{(\text{SG\&A}_t / \text{Sales}_t)}{(\text{SG\&A}_{t-1} / \text{Sales}_{t-1})}$ $>1.0$: Decreasing administrative efficiency.
LVGI Leverage Index: $\frac{\text{Leverage}_t}{\text{Leverage}_{t-1}}$ $>1.0$: Increasing debt relative to assets creates risk of covenant breaches.
TATA Total Accruals to Total Assets: $\frac{\text{Net Income}_t - \text{CFO}_t}{\text{Total Assets}_t}$ High positive value indicates earnings are driven by non-cash accruals rather than cash collections.

18. Integration of FSA Techniques

Synthesizing analysis across multiple financial statements to normalize metrics and build reliable multi-period valuation forecasts.

Framework for Normalizing Financial Statements

  1. Inventory Normalization: Convert LIFO inventory and COGS to FIFO values using the LIFO Reserve.
  2. Off-Balance-Sheet & Operating Lease Adjustments: Bring historical commitments onto the balance sheet.
  3. Pension Adjustments: Reclassify operating vs financing pension components; eliminate corridor smoothing for US GAAP.
  4. Goodwill & Intangible Adjustments: Subtract goodwill from equity to calculate Tangible Book Value ($TBV$) for conservative leverage analysis.
  5. Non-Recurring Items Removal: Strip out restructuring charges, gains/losses on asset sales, and foreign currency translation spikes when estimating baseline run-rate operating income.

01. Fixed Income Essentials & Bond Pricing Mechanics

A bond represents a contractual debt obligation between the issuer (borrower) and the investor (creditor). The fundamental value of any default-free fixed-income instrument equals the present value of its future cash flows discounted at the market discount rate (YTM).

The Universal Bond Valuation Equation

Fundamental Bond Pricing Formula
$$PV = \sum_{t=1}^N \frac{PMT}{(1 + r)^t} + \frac{FV}{(1 + r)^N}$$ $$\text{Where: } PMT = \text{Coupon payment per period}, \quad FV = \text{Face (Par) value}, \quad r = \text{Market discount rate per period}$$

Full Price (Dirty Price) vs Flat Price (Clean Price)

In secondary bond markets, transactions rarely settle precisely on a coupon payment date. The buyer must compensate the seller for accrued interest earned from the last coupon date to settlement date:

Clean vs Dirty Bond Pricing & Accrued Interest
$$PV^{\text{Full}} = PV^{\text{Flat}} + AI$$ $$AI = PMT \times \left( \frac{t}{T} \right)$$ $$\text{Where: } t = \text{Days accrued since prior coupon}, \quad T = \text{Total days in coupon period}$$
  • Actual/Actual Convention: Standard for government bonds. Exact calendar days elapsed divided by actual days in coupon period.
  • 30/360 Convention: Standard for corporate and municipal bonds. Assumes 30 days per month and 360 days per year.

Matrix Pricing for Illiquid & Unrated Bonds

When a target bond is illiquid or newly issued without market quotes, analysts utilize Matrix Pricing (linear interpolation of yields on comparable liquid benchmark bonds matching maturity and credit quality) to establish the appropriate discounting yield.

02. Term Structure of Interest Rates & Yield Curves

The term structure of interest rates describes the relationship between maturity tenors and yields for benchmark bonds of identical creditworthiness. A single discount rate (YTM) for all cash flows is a simplification; rigorous valuation requires discounting each cash flow at its specific spot rate.

Spot Rates & Curve Bootstrapping

The Spot Rate ($S_t$) is the yield to maturity on a zero-coupon bond maturing at period $t$. Bootstrapping systematically extracts zero-coupon spot rates from par yield curves:

Spot Rate Valuation & Bootstrapping Equation
$$PV = \frac{PMT}{1 + S_1} + \frac{PMT}{(1 + S_2)^2} + \cdots + \frac{PMT + FV}{(1 + S_N)^N}$$ $$1 = \frac{c}{1 + S_1} + \frac{c}{(1 + S_2)^2} + \frac{1 + c}{(1 + S_3)^3} \implies S_3 = \left( \frac{1 + c}{1 - \frac{c}{1+S_1} - \frac{c}{(1+S_2)^2}} \right)^{1/3} - 1$$

Forward Rates & Forward Rate Parity

A forward rate $f(A, B-A)$ is an interest rate agreed upon today for a loan beginning at future period $A$ and maturing at period $B$. Under no-arbitrage conditions:

Forward Rate Parity Identity
$$(1 + S_B)^B = (1 + S_A)^A \times [1 + f(A, B-A)]^{B-A}$$ $$[1 + f(1, 1)] = \frac{(1 + S_2)^2}{(1 + S_1)^1}$$
Visual 1: Benchmark Spot Curve vs Implied Forward Curve
When the spot yield curve is upward sloping, the forward curve always lies above the spot curve ($f(t-1, 1) > S_t > y_{par}$).

Term Structure Theories

Hypothesis Core Principle Yield Curve Interpretation
Pure Expectations Theory Forward rates are unbiased predictors of future spot rates. No risk premium required for longer maturities. Upward slope indicates market expects future short-term interest rates to rise.
Liquidity Preference Theory Investors demand a liquidity premium ($L_t$) for tying up funds in longer-term, less liquid bonds. Curves slope upward naturally even if expected future spot rates are flat or slightly declining.
Segmented Markets Theory Yields at each maturity are determined independently by supply and demand of institutional habitat participants. Shape is determined by supply-demand imbalances across market segments (e.g. pension funds in 30Y).
Preferred Habitat Theory Market participants have preferred maturities but will cross segments if yield premium is sufficiently attractive. Humps and twists reflect market-clearing risk premiums required to induce cross-segment capital migration.

03. Yield Measures, Benchmark Spreads & Option-Adjusted Spreads

Credit risk, liquidity risk, and taxation cause corporate bonds to trade at a spread above default-free benchmark government bonds.

Key Spread Definitions

  • G-Spread (Government Spread): Yield spread between a corporate bond and an interpolated government benchmark bond of identical maturity.
  • I-Spread (Interpolated Spread): Yield spread over standard interbank swap benchmark rates (MRR / SOFR swap rates).
  • Zero-Volatility Spread (Z-Spread): Constant basis point spread added to each spot rate on the benchmark zero curve to equate the present value of bond cash flows to its market price: $$PV = \sum_{t=1}^N \frac{CF_t}{(1 + S_t + Z)^t}$$
  • Option-Adjusted Spread (OAS): The spread isolated after stripping out the cost of embedded options (calls, puts). Measures pure credit and liquidity risk: $$\text{Option Cost (bps)} = Z\text{-spread} - OAS$$ $$\text{For a Callable Bond: } Z\text{-spread} > OAS \implies \text{Option Cost} > 0$$ $$\text{For a Putable Bond: } Z\text{-spread} < OAS \implies \text{Option Cost} < 0$$

04. Interest Rate Risk: Duration, Convexity & Sensitivity

Duration measures a bond's price sensitivity to changes in benchmark interest rates. Convexity measures the rate of change of duration, providing a second-order curvature adjustment for large interest rate shocks.

Macaulay, Modified & Effective Duration

Duration Formulas & Relationships
$$MacDur = \sum_{t=1}^N \left[ t \times \frac{CF_t / (1 + y)^t}{PV} \right]$$ $$ModDur = \frac{MacDur}{1 + y / k} \quad (k = \text{compounding frequency per year})$$ $$EffDur = \frac{PV_- - PV_+}{2 \times \Delta y \times PV_0} \quad (\text{Mandatory for bonds with embedded options})$$

Convexity & The Combined Price Approximation

Because the price-yield relationship of a straight bond is convex (curves upward), a linear duration estimate underestimates price increases when yields fall and overestimates price declines when yields rise:

Full Taylor-Series Price Change Approximation
$$\% \Delta PV \approx -ModDur \times \Delta y + \frac{1}{2} \times Convexity \times (\Delta y)^2$$ $$ApproxConvexity = \frac{PV_- + PV_+ - 2PV_0}{(\Delta y)^2 \times PV_0}$$
Visual 2: Price-Yield Convexity vs Linear Duration Approximation
The tangible benefit of positive convexity: the bond price rises more when yields drop than it falls when yields increase by the same magnitude.

Key Rate Duration (KRD)

Key rate duration measures bond price sensitivity to a 100 bps shift at a single maturity point on the spot curve while holding all other points constant. The sum of all key rate durations equals the effective duration for a parallel shift:

$$EffDur = \sum_{i=1}^M KRD_i$$

05. Bonds with Embedded Options & Binomial Trees

Bonds containing call, put, or conversion features cannot be valued with standard yield-to-maturity discounting due to cash flow uncertainty contingent on path-dependent interest rate outcomes.

Callable vs Putable Bond Valuation

Embedded Option Decomposition
$$V_{\text{Callable Bond}} = V_{\text{Straight Bond}} - V_{\text{Call Option}}$$ $$V_{\text{Putable Bond}} = V_{\text{Straight Bond}} + V_{\text{Put Option}}$$
Negative Convexity Trap: As benchmark yields decline, the probability of the issuer calling the bond increases dramatically. The price of a callable bond compression ceiling is reached at the call price. At low yields, callable bonds exhibit negative convexity (falling yields yield diminishing price gains).

Binomial Interest Rate Tree Backward Induction

A binomial tree models interest rate evolution under lognormal volatility: $r_{1, u} = r_{1, d} e^{2\sigma}$. Valuation proceeds backwards from maturity ($T$) to node 0:

Backward Induction Valuation Node Equation
$$V_{\text{node}} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{V_{u} + PMT}{1 + r_{\text{node}}} + \frac{V_{d} + PMT}{1 + r_{\text{node}}} \right]$$ $$\text{Callable Node Decision: } V = \min(\text{Calculated Node Value}, \text{Call Price})$$ $$\text{Putable Node Decision: } V = \max(\text{Calculated Node Value}, \text{Put Price})$$

06. Credit Analysis, Expected Loss & Structural Models

Credit analysis evaluates an issuer's default risk and creditworthiness. Credit risk comprises two core components: default probability and recovery rate upon default.

Expected Loss Mathematics

Expected Loss & Recovery Rate
$$\text{Expected Loss} = \text{Probability of Default (PD)} \times \text{Loss Given Default (LGD)}$$ $$\text{LGD} = 1 - \text{Recovery Rate (RR)}$$ $$\text{Present Value of Expected Loss (CVA)} = PV_{\text{Default-Free}} - PV_{\text{Risky}}$$

Structural vs Reduced Form Credit Models

Attribute Structural Models (Merton 1974) Reduced Form Models
Core Foundation Company's balance sheet structure: equity is a European call option on firm assets ($V_A$) with strike equal to debt face value ($K$). Statistical intensity process where default occurs as an exogenous Poisson jump process.
Default Condition Default occurs at maturity $T$ if total asset value falls below debt obligations: $V_A(T) < K$. Default can occur randomly at any instant prior to maturity based on macro hazard rates.
Inputs Required Market value of firm assets, asset return volatility ($\sigma_A$), balance sheet debt levels. Market credit spreads, macroeconomic covariates, historical rating transition matrices.

07. Asset-Backed (ABS) & Mortgage-Backed Securities (MBS)

Securitization pools illiquid financial assets (residential mortgages, auto loans, credit card debt) and converts them into tradable marketable securities through a bankruptcy-remote Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV).

Prepayment Risk: Contraction vs Extension Risk

  • Contraction Risk: Occurs when interest rates decline significantly. Homeowners refinance mortgages at lower rates, accelerating principal prepayments. MBS investors receive early principal and are forced to reinvest at lower prevailing rates, shortening maturity.
  • Extension Risk: Occurs when interest rates rise. Homeowners delay moving or refinancing, slowing prepayments. Investors remain locked into below-market coupon payments, extending average life.

Prepayment Metrics: SMM & CPR

Prepayment Rate Identities
$$SMM = \frac{\text{Prepayment in Month } t}{\text{Beginning Mortgage Balance} - \text{Scheduled Principal}}$$ $$CPR = 1 - (1 - SMM)^{12} \iff SMM = 1 - (1 - CPR)^{1/12}$$

Collateralized Mortgage Obligations (CMO) Tranching

  • Sequential-Pay Tranches: Principal payments retire tranches in sequential order (Tranche A first, then B, then C). Early tranches absorb contraction risk; later tranches absorb extension risk.
  • PAC & Support Tranches: Planned Amortization Class (PAC) tranches provide stable cash flows within a specified prepayment collar. The support tranche absorbs prepayments above or below the band, exhibiting high volatility.

08. Master Fixed Income Formula Cheat Sheet

Direct lookup formula card for rapid calculation during CFA Level 1 and Level 2 exam problem solving:

Topic Metric / Formula KaTeX Mathematical Formulation Notes & Key Usage
Pricing Full Bond Price $$PV^{\text{Full}} = PV^{\text{Flat}} + AI$$ Clean price plus accrued interest based on day-count convention.
Curves Forward Rate Parity $$(1 + S_B)^B = (1 + S_A)^A \times [1 + f(A, B-A)]^{B-A}$$ No-arbitrage relationship linking spot and forward rates.
Risk Modified Duration $$ModDur = \frac{MacDur}{1 + y / k}$$ Measures percentage price change per 100 bps shift in yield.
Risk Convexity Adjustment $$\% \Delta PV \approx -ModDur(\Delta y) + \frac{1}{2} Convexity(\Delta y)^2$$ Second-order Taylor expansion correcting for curvature.
Spreads Option Cost (bps) $$\text{Option Cost} = Z\text{-spread} - OAS$$ Positive for callable bonds; negative for putable bonds.
Trees Binomial Node Value $$V = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{V_u + C}{1 + r_u} + \frac{V_d + C}{1 + r_d} \right]$$ Backward induction node pricing using 50/50 risk-neutral branch probabilities.
Credit Expected Loss $$\text{ExpLoss} = PD \times (1 - RR)$$ Default probability times loss given default.
Prepayment SMM from CPR $$SMM = 1 - (1 - CPR)^{1/12}$$ Monthly equivalent prepayment rate.

01. Market Organization, Security Trading & Indexes

Financial markets channel capital from savers to productive investment. Analysts must evaluate market order execution mechanisms, leverage trading limits, and benchmark index construction.

Margin Transactions & Margin Call Pricing

When buying securities on margin, the investor borrows part of the purchase price from the broker. The Margin Call Price ($P$) is the stock price below which the broker requires additional equity collateral:

Margin Call Trigger Price Formula
$$P = P_0 \times \left( \frac{1 - \text{Initial Margin}}{1 - \text{Maintenance Margin}} \right)$$ $$\text{Where: } P_0 = \text{Initial purchase price}, \quad IM = \text{Initial equity margin %}, \quad MM = \text{Maintenance margin %}$$

Equity Index Construction Methodologies

Weighting Method Weighting Basis Stock Split Impact Prominent Example
Price-Weighted Price per share divided by index divisor: $w_i = P_i / \sum P_k$. Requires divisor adjustment; high-priced stocks have disproportionate influence. Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA), Nikkei 225.
Value-Weighted (Market-Cap) Total market capitalization: $w_i = (P_i Q_i) / \sum (P_k Q_k)$. Often float-adjusted. No divisor adjustment required for stock splits; mirrors true aggregate wealth. S&P 500, MSCI World, FTSE 100.
Equal-Weighted Each constituent stock receives identical weight: $w_i = 1 / N$. Requires frequent rebalancing as stock prices diverge; small-cap tilt. S&P 500 Equal Weight Index.

02. Industry & Competitive Strategy Analysis

Industry structure drives fundamental return on invested capital (ROIC). Michael Porter's Five Forces framework analyzes the competitive intensity and sustainable pricing power of an industry.

Porter's Five Forces Framework

  • Threat of New Entrants: High barriers to entry (economies of scale, patents, high switching costs) protect economic profits.
  • Bargaining Power of Buyers: Concentrated buyers or standardized commodity products reduce pricing power.
  • Bargaining Power of Suppliers: Fragmented buyers dealing with few specialized suppliers face high input costs.
  • Threat of Substitute Products: Close substitutes cap pricing power and elastic demand.
  • Rivalry Among Existing Competitors: Intense price competition occurs in fragmented industries with high exit barriers and slow growth.

Industry Life Cycle Stages

  1. Embryonic: Slow growth, high startup costs, unproven customer demand.
  2. Growth: Rapidly rising demand, improving profitability, falling production costs.
  3. Shakeout: Growth slows, overcapacity develops, price wars force weaker firms out.
  4. Mature: Slower growth matching GDP, consolidated oligopoly, focus on efficiency.
  5. Decline: Negative demand growth due to technological substitution.

03. Dividend Discount Models & Multi-Stage Valuation

The Dividend Discount Model (DDM) values common stock as the present value of all expected future cash dividend payments discounted at the required return on equity ($r$).

Gordon Growth Model & Sustainable Growth Rate

Constant Growth DDM (Gordon Growth)
$$V_0 = \frac{D_1}{r - g} = \frac{D_0 (1 + g)}{r - g} \quad (\text{Condition: } r > g)$$ $$g = b \times ROE = (1 - \text{Dividend Payout Ratio}) \times ROE$$

Present Value of Growth Opportunities (PVGO)

A firm's stock value can be decomposed into the value of its current no-growth earnings stream plus the net present value of profitable growth investments:

PVGO Decomposition
$$V_0 = \frac{E_1}{r} + PVGO \implies PVGO = V_0 - \frac{E_1}{r}$$

The H-Model for Linearly Transitioning Growth

The H-Model values a firm experiencing high initial growth ($g_S$) that transitions linearly over half-life $H$ (years $= 2H$) to a sustainable long-term rate ($g_L$):

H-Model Valuation Equation
$$V_0 = \frac{D_0 (1 + g_L)}{r - g_L} + \frac{D_0 \times H \times (g_S - g_L)}{r - g_L}$$
Visual 1: DDM Valuation Sensitivity to Cost of Equity & Long-Term Growth
Demonstrates asymptotic intrinsic value expansion as the required return $r$ approaches the perpetual growth rate $g$.

04. Free Cash Flow Valuation (FCFF & FCFE)

Free cash flow models are superior when firms do not pay dividends, dividend policy does not reflect underlying profitability, or an acquiring firm seeks control of total operational cash flow.

Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF) Derivations

FCFF Multi-Source Accounting Identities
$$\text{From Net Income: } FCFF = NI + NCC + \text{Interest}(1 - T) - FCInv - WCInv$$ $$\text{From CFO: } FCFF = CFO + \text{Interest}(1 - T) - FCInv$$ $$\text{From EBIT: } FCFF = EBIT(1 - T) + Dep - FCInv - WCInv$$ $$\text{From EBITDA: } FCFF = EBITDA(1 - T) + (Dep \times T) - FCInv - WCInv$$

Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE) Derivations

FCFE Formulas & Net Borrowing Integration
$$FCFE = FCFF - \text{Interest}(1 - T) + \text{Net Borrowing}$$ $$FCFE = NI + NCC - FCInv - WCInv + \text{Net Borrowing}$$ $$FCFE = CFO - FCInv + \text{Net Borrowing}$$ $$\text{Where: } \text{Net Borrowing} = \text{New Debt Issued} - \text{Principal Repayments}$$
Visual 2: Cash Flow Waterfall Bridge from Operational Profit to Free Cash Flow
Step-by-step conversion of EBITDA down to Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF) and Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE).

05. Market Multiples & Valuation Ratios

Relative valuation compares a company's market price multiplier against comparable peer benchmarks or historic averages. Justified multiples are derived directly from fundamental discounted cash flow economics.

Justified Multipliers Derived from Fundamentals

Core Fundamental Justified Multiplier Identities
$$\text{Justified Leading P/E: } \frac{P_0}{E_1} = \frac{1 - b}{r - g}$$ $$\text{Justified Trailing P/E: } \frac{P_0}{E_0} = \frac{(1 - b)(1 + g)}{r - g}$$ $$\text{Justified Price-to-Book (P/B): } \frac{P_0}{B_0} = \frac{ROE - g}{r - g}$$ $$\text{Justified Price-to-Sales (P/S): } \frac{P_0}{S_0} = \frac{\text{Net Margin} \times (1 - b)(1 + g)}{r - g}$$

Enterprise Value Multipliers

Enterprise Value ($EV$) measures total market value of core operations independent of capital structure financing:

Enterprise Value Accounting Identity
$$EV = \text{Market Value of Common Equity} + \text{Total Debt} + \text{Preferred Stock} + \text{Minority Interest} - \text{Cash & Equivalents}$$

06. Residual Income Valuation & Clean Surplus Accounting

Residual Income (Economic Profit) equals net income in excess of the accounting equity charge for the cost of equity capital ($r \times B_{t-1}$).

Residual Income Valuation Equation

Universal Residual Income Model
$$V_0 = B_0 + \sum_{t=1}^\infty \frac{RI_t}{(1 + r)^t}$$ $$RI_t = NI_t - (r \times B_{t-1}) = (ROE_t - r) \times B_{t-1}$$
Clean Surplus Relation: The balance sheet book value must reconcile perfectly through earnings and dividends: $$B_t = B_{t-1} + NI_t - Div_t$$ Items bypassing the income statement through Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI)—such as foreign currency translation adjustments or unrealized gains on OCI securities—violate clean surplus and require analyst normalization.

Continuing Residual Income & Persistence Factor ($\omega$)

Under competitive market dynamics, supernormal returns decay over time to normal returns ($ROE \to r$):

Terminal Value with Persistence Decay ($\omega$)
$$PV(\text{Continuing RI at } T-1) = \frac{RI_T}{1 + r - \omega}$$ $$\text{Where } \omega \in [0, 1]: \quad \omega = 1.0 \implies \text{Perpetual RI}, \quad \omega = 0.0 \implies \text{Instant Return to Cost of Equity}$$

07. Private Company Valuation & Normalization Adjustments

Private company valuation requires adjusting financial statements for non-market transactions and quantifying illiquidity and control differentials.

Financial Statement Normalization

  • Officer/Owner Compensation: Replace non-market excessive or below-market salaries with fair market executive compensation.
  • Non-Operating Assets & Expenses: Segregate excess cash, corporate personal aircraft, or real estate assets held for speculation.
  • Related-Party Transactions: Re-align intercompany lease agreements to market rents.

Valuation Discounts & Premiums

Control and Marketability Discount Interaction
$$\text{Total Combined Discount} = 1 - (1 - DLOC) \times (1 - DLOM)$$ $$DLOC = 1 - \left( \frac{1}{1 + \text{Control Premium}} \right)$$ $$\text{Where: } DLOC = \text{Discount for Lack of Control}, \quad DLOM = \text{Discount for Lack of Marketability}$$

08. Master Equity Valuation Formula Cheat Sheet

Direct reference formula cheat sheet for rapid multi-model valuation problem solving:

Model Metric Name KaTeX Mathematical Formulation Primary Exam Usage
DDM Gordon Growth Value $$V_0 = \frac{D_1}{r - g} = \frac{D_0 (1 + g)}{r - g}$$ Mature, steady dividend-paying corporations.
DDM Sustainable Growth $$g = b \times ROE = (1 - PR) \times ROE$$ Internal equity reinvestment rate.
DDM H-Model Value $$V_0 = \frac{D_0 (1 + g_L)}{r - g_L} + \frac{D_0 H (g_S - g_L)}{r - g_L}$$ High growth transitioning linearly to long-term rate.
DCF FCFF from CFO $$FCFF = CFO + \text{Interest}(1 - T) - FCInv$$ Fastest calculation when Cash Flow Statement is provided.
DCF FCFE from FCFF $$FCFE = FCFF - \text{Interest}(1 - T) + \text{Net Borrowing}$$ Direct equity cash flow valuation.
Multipliers Justified P/B $$\frac{P_0}{B_0} = \frac{ROE - g}{r - g}$$ Values capital-intensive financial and asset-heavy firms.
Residual Income Residual Income Value $$V_0 = B_0 + \sum_{t=1}^\infty \frac{(ROE_t - r) B_{t-1}}{(1 + r)^t}$$ Values firms with negative cash flows or non-dividend payers.
Private Total Discount $$\text{Total Disc} = 1 - (1 - DLOC)(1 - DLOM)$$ Multiplicative interaction of lack of control and marketability.

CFA Exam Master Formula Cheatsheet
Bond Price: $$PV = \sum_{t=1}^N \frac{PMT}{(1+r)^t} + \frac{FV}{(1+r)^N}$$
Macaulay & Modified Duration: $$ModDur = \frac{MacDur}{1+y}, \quad \%\Delta P \approx -ModDur \times \Delta y + \frac{1}{2} Conv \times (\Delta y)^2$$
Two-Stage DDM: $$V_0 = \sum_{t=1}^n \frac{D_0(1+g_S)^t}{(1+r)^t} + \frac{D_0(1+g_S)^n(1+g_L)}{(r - g_L)(1+r)^n}$$
DuPont 5-Way: $$ROE = \frac{NI}{EBT} \times \frac{EBT}{EBIT} \times \frac{EBIT}{Rev} \times \frac{Rev}{Assets} \times \frac{Assets}{Equity}$$
FCFF from Net Income: $$FCFF = NI + NCC + Int(1 - T) - FCInv - WCInv$$
